extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media scholars, and policymakers concerned with news quality and democratic effects
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for news reporting quality, with emphasis on the watchdog role, tone (negative vs. positive), investigative depth, sourcing practices, audience preferences, and appropriate balance between hard and soft news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical journalism requires thorough scrutiny and deep investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: In theory, critical journalism requires the journalist to thoroughly scrutinize the behavior of officials and bring to light their shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-notch investigative journalism 'ordinarily takes a great deal of effort to determine the validity of a politician’s claim or to prove instances of wrongdoing or ineptitude.' The 24-hour news cycle and resource/time constraints make it nearly impossible to regularly engage in high-quality investigative reporting; Watergate is cited as an example of successful deep investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative reporting requires substantial time and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality investigative journalism takes an amount of time that most journalists are not normally allowed to devote to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because deep investigation is time-consuming, newsrooms must allocate time and resources if they are to reliably uncover wrongdoing; without that investment, critical claims often lack verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid supplying criticism by rote through adversary-sourced counter-claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Much negative content is supplied through journalists’ use of sources rather than deep investigation; reporters often turn to adversaries to attack a statement or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: inserting a counter-claim from an adversary instead of conducting careful assessment. The report notes this has become routine and describes it as a degeneration of critical journalism that increases the rate of criticism without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog role: distinguish genuine abuse from small errors of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A watchdog press must have the judgment to distinguish real abuse from officials’ small errors of judgment and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to make this distinction 'poisons the well,' weakening public trust. The Lewinsky coverage is cited as an instance where sensational, lurid reporting rooted in hearsay caused the public to view the press as unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give proper voice to newsmakers and report what government does well
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible journalism should give proper voice to newsmakers, pay sufficient attention to what government is doing well, and assess politicians’ failings by reasonable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balances the watchdog function with fairness: not ignoring wrongdoing, but not turning the agenda over to scandal or making media the focus instead of newsmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive negativity and sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should avoid relentless negativity, sensationalism, and intrusive reporting; excessive negativity reduces political trust and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show a majority believe public-affairs reporting has become too negative, sensational, and intrusive. Negative coverage has risen dramatically and correlates with declines in trust in government and interest in public affairs. The press’s skepticism is both protective and seen as an obstacle to governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tone and content: match tone to story type (hard vs. soft news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone matters differently for soft news and hard news: negative headlines attract more interest for soft news, while for hard news the positive versions sometimes draw more interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline Test: negative headlines attracted more interest overall, but the difference was small and content mattered more than tone. For hard-news topics, positive headlines drew slightly more interest. Editors should consider story type when choosing headline tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize substantive public-affairs reporting to build sustainable audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Balanced public-affairs reporting (substantive rather than entertainment/shock) is the best long-term strategy for building and sustaining a news audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft and negative news may yield short-term attention, but over time they erode interest in news and political engagement. 'What is good for democracy is also good for the press.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize reporter-centered coverage; center newsmakers’ words and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should avoid making themselves the focus of coverage at the expense of newsmakers’ words and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2000 campaign coverage reporters spoke six minutes for every minute candidates’ words could be heard. Such reporter-centered coverage involves sweeping judgments and diminishes the centrality of primary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a negativity bias (the press’s real bias) rather than simple partisan bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The contemporary press’s dominant bias is a tendency to report what is wrong with politics and politicians rather than partisan favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideological premise presumes most politicians are incompetent or deceptive; the recommendation is to correct this negativity bias and report what is right as well as wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect privacy and avoid intrusive coverage of private lives unless clearly newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should exercise restraint regarding officials’ private lives; excessive intrusion (e.g., 'bedroom behavior') is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expansion of intrusive private-life coverage reflects declining respect and contributes to perceptions that the press is overly sensational and unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-oriented criteria for news value (what consumers find important)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey-based list of what audiences rate important in news: lively/enjoyable; fits easily into daily schedule; timely and up to date; provides information to understand public affairs; provides information helpful in daily life; tells about good and bad things happening to ordinary people; stirs emotions; is substantial rather than sensational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items (from SN-19) indicate news producers should weigh timeliness, informativeness, practicality, emotional engagement, entertainment, and substance when designing news offerings; 'busy' people prefer tightly packaged hard news and place a premium on public affairs information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectival quality metrics for news evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers judge news by paired adjectives: fair vs biased; negative vs positive; interesting vs boring; serious vs sensational; informative vs uninformative; superficial vs thorough; accurate vs misleading; depressing vs uplifting; enjoyable vs not enjoyable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit evaluative dimensions (from SN-17) provide a checklist for assessing perceived news quality and tone across multiple axes such as fairness, accuracy, depth, and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline/content selection should prioritize substantive content over shock value
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is often more important than tone in driving interest: a headline about Middle East conflict drew more interest (regardless of positive/negative framing) than one about drug charges for a pro football player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While negative headlines can attract attention, editors should prioritize topic salience and relevance over merely choosing a negative frame to increase interest.
